title: Lab: Hash Table From Scratch
summary: Build a real hash table from a plain array — your own hash function, your own collision handling, your own resizing — and put every guarantee that theory promised to an actual, measured test.

references.label: Sedgewick & Wayne — Algorithms, 4th ed. Companion Site

title: Lab: Percolation — Union-Find in Practice
summary: Princeton's own famous union-find assignment: model a grid of sites opening one at a time, and use union-find to answer, after every single opening, whether the grid now percolates top to bottom.

title: Lab: Boggle-Style Word Search — Trie in Practice

related.label: Tries: Prefix Trees for String Keys

summary: Load a large dictionary into a trie, then search a letter grid for every valid word — the exact prefix-pruning trick a trie enables, and a hash-set-based version to measure why it isn't fast enough.

references.label: Sedgewick & Wayne — Algorithms, 4th ed. Companion Site

title: Lab: Dijkstra's Shortest Path, Implemented
summary: Implement Dijkstra's algorithm for real, on a real weighted graph, backed by the heap already built — and verify its output against a graph small enough to check by hand.

references.label: Sedgewick & Wayne — Algorithms, 4th ed. Companion Site

title: Lab: A* Pathfinding
summary: Dijkstra explores blindly outward in every direction — A* adds a heuristic estimate of remaining distance, exploring toward the goal instead, and stays exact as long as that heuristic never overestimates.

references.label: Red Blob Games — Introduction to A*

title: Lab: Shortest Common Ancestor in a DAG
summary: Princeton's WordNet-style problem: given a directed acyclic graph of hypernym relationships, find the shortest ancestral path connecting any two nodes — two BFS traversals combined into one real answer.

references.label: Sedgewick & Wayne — Algorithms, 4th ed. Companion Site

title: Lab: PageRank via Power Iteration
summary: The same PageRank already solved as a 4-page toy eigenvector problem — reimplemented the way Google's original paper actually describes computing it at scale: no eigendecomposition, just repeated matrix-vector multiplication until it settles.

references.label: Brin & Page — The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine
Sedgewick & Wayne — Algorithms, 4th ed. Companion Site

title: Lab: Kd-Trees for 2D Range Search

related.label: Binary Search Trees: Search, Insert, Delete

summary: A BST that alternates which coordinate it splits on at each level — the natural, already-familiar tree-search idea, extended to answer "which points fall inside this rectangle" far faster than checking every point.

references.label: Sedgewick & Wayne — Algorithms, 4th ed. Companion Site

title: Lab: B-Trees, Implemented

related.label: Comparing AVL and Red-Black Trees in Practice

summary: AVL and red-black trees stay balanced by keeping at most 2 children per node — a B-tree instead lets each node hold many keys and many children, the specific shape that makes it the structure real databases and filesystems actually use.

title: Capstone: Empirical Performance Analysis
summary: Every Big-O claim made across this entire curriculum, put to an actual timed test — measuring real running times against growing input sizes for the structures built in this lab, and checking whether the numbers actually behave the way the theory promised.

references.label: Sedgewick & Wayne — Algorithms, 4th ed. Companion Site
